clue.text: Notes left for the newsboy?

parts.note: banknotes left out to pay the lad who delivers the daily paper could be called cash for the paper

explanation.surface: Someone leaves a few written messages out for the newspaper delivery boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notes' seems to mean written messages, but it means banknotes, and the newsboy delivers papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Banknotes are currency printed on paper rather than coins.

clue.text: Stops on the way for refreshments?

definitions.text: Stops on the way for refreshments?

parts.words: Stops on the way for refreshments?
parts.note: places a traveller halts for a drink, but also places that stop people going on their way

explanation.surface: A traveller breaks a journey for a snack or a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Taverns are where a journey is broken for a pint.

clue.text: An East European electrical terminal

definitions.meaning: either end of a battery, positive or negative

explanation.definitionFit: A native of Poland is so called, and a battery has a positive and negative terminal of the same name.

clue.text: He gets into the Royal Society before us, the monkey!

indicators.note: the first part comes ahead of the next word in the answer
the word he gets into, so it sits inside the abbreviation for the society

parts.note: RS is the abbreviation for the Royal Society, Britain's scientific academy
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man joins Britain's scientific academy ahead of us, and turns out to be a monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes 'the monkey' read as a jibe at the man, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhesus is a macaque, a species of Asian primate much used in research.

clue.text: Britain's flow of capital affectionately personified

definitions.text: Britain's flow of capital affectionately personified

parts.words: Britain's flow of capital affectionately personified
parts.note: the river through London, pictured as a bearded old man in a fond nickname; 'flow of capital' looks like money

explanation.surface: Money moving around Britain's economy is spoken of fondly as a person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flow of capital' suggests finance, but it is the river flowing through the capital, London.
explanation.definitionFit: The river through London is personified in folklore and art as a venerable bearded figure.

clue.text: Susan returning to the North-from here by train, perhaps?

indicators.note: Susan's short form comes back, so it is read from right to left

parts.note: Sue is a short form of the name Susan
taken as written

explanation.surface: Susan heads back up north, travelling by train.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic hint: a London terminus from which trains run north.
explanation.definitionFit: London's Euston is the mainline station where trains for the north-west and Scotland start, so one may set out from there.

clue.text: Does evangelical work

definitions.meaning: the New Testament book recording the Apostles' missionary deeds

explanation.definitionFit: To perform is to carry out deeds, and the book of the Apostles after the Gospels bears that title.

clue.text: Might be disposed to give Horace some land

indicators.note: the letters could be laid out in another order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone may be inclined to hand over a plot of land to Horace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposed' suggests inclined to give, but it means arranged differently.
explanation.definitionFit: To disembark from a ship is to reach the shore.

clue.text: The black-market transactions Wilberforce campaigned against

definitions.text: The black-market transactions Wilberforce campaigned against

parts.words: The black-market transactions Wilberforce campaigned against
parts.note: trade in black Africans as human property, which William Wilberforce fought to abolish; black market looks like illegal dealing

explanation.surface: An MP campaigns against illicit dealings.
explanation.walkthrough: William Wilberforce was the British MP who led the campaign to abolish the trade in enslaved Africans.
explanation.definitionFit: Commerce in human beings, abolished in the British Empire largely through Wilberforce's efforts.

clue.text: A Norse god to confound? Nonsense!

parts.note: Balder is the Norse god of light, son of Odin
dash, as in 'dash it!', is a mild oath meaning confound it

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea of cursing a Norse deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean rubbish talk, empty and senseless speech.

clue.text: She makes a come-back at the end of the programme

indicators.note: the letters picked return, so they are read from right to left
the letters taken lie in the final stretch of the word programme

explanation.surface: A performer returns at the close of a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The last four letters of 'programme' are AMME; turned round they give a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, such as Jane Austen's heroine, stands for a woman.

clue.text: Express delivery-man

parts.note: looks like a courier, but means a cricketer whose deliveries (balls) are quick

explanation.surface: A courier who brings parcels in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a delivery is a ball bowled; a quick bowler sends down express deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricketer who bowls at high pace is so called.

clue.text: Lights up in a big way after dark?

definitions.text: Lights up in a big way after dark?

parts.words: Lights up in a big way after dark?
parts.note: the heavens lit up with countless points of light at night

explanation.surface: Something is lit up grandly once night falls.
explanation.definitionFit: A clear night heaven with its stars shining is lit on a vast scale.

clue.text: A superintendent who doesn't mind when he takes a day off

definitions.text: A superintendent who doesn't mind when he takes a day off

parts.words: A superintendent who doesn't mind when he takes a day off
parts.note: a keeper of a museum collection minds the exhibits, so on a day off he is not minding them

explanation.surface: A relaxed manager is happy to take time off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doesn't mind' seems to mean is untroubled, but it means is not looking after the collection.
explanation.definitionFit: A museum or gallery keeper superintends a collection.

clue.text: A boxer who takes pleasure in holidaying overseas

definitions.meaning: a fighter in the cruiserweight division

definitions.text: who takes pleasure in holidaying overseas
definitions.meaning: a holidaymaker on a pleasure voyage

explanation.definitionFit: A cruiserweight is a boxing class, and someone on a sea voyage for pleasure is a holidaymaker afloat.

clue.text: Gives an account of the undoing of Laertes?

indicators.note: the name is taken apart and its letters put back in another order

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone narrates the downfall of Laertes, Hamlet's rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Laertes is the character killed in the final duel of Shakespeare's Hamlet, so 'undoing' looks like his ruin.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate or tell a story is to give an account.

clue.text: They pretend there's gold in 6

indicators.note: the metal goes into the answer to clue 6, which wraps around it

parts.note: the answer to 6 across, does
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Someone claims there is gold hidden in clue 6.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage players make believe for a living.

clue.text: Issue an annulment order?

parts.note: to declare something void, as an order cancelling it would

explanation.surface: A court hands down a decree cancelling a marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: To nullify or cancel is what an order of annulment does.

clue.text: Frightfully bad conditions

parts.note: 'frightfully' as in very, and 'conditions' as in the state of the sky outdoors

explanation.surface: Things are awful all round.
explanation.definitionFit: Storms, rain and gales make for awful conditions outdoors.

clue.text: He has to be among the other ranks

indicators.note: the verb is placed amid the letters for the soldiers

parts.note: OR is the military abbreviation for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
to live is to exist, to be

explanation.surface: A man insists he belongs with the ordinary soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is the definition, a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy's name, like Dickens's Twist, stands for a man.

clue.text: Highland gorge Vera roams about in

indicators.note: the letters wander and settle in a new order

parts.note: fodder taken as written
fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman called Vera wanders around inside a Scottish gorge.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep narrow valley is a gorge.

clue.text: Took a close look, creating deeper confusion

indicators.note: the word is jumbled so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stared hard and only became more baffled.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare intently, squinting to see, is to look closely.

clue.text: Its inmates get time to reflect on their misdeeds

definitions.text: Its inmates get time to reflect on their misdeeds

parts.words: Its inmates get time to reflect on their misdeeds
parts.note: 'get time' means are sentenced, which gives them leisure to think over their crimes

explanation.surface: People in some institution are given time to think about what they did wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A jail holds convicts serving a term for their crimes.

clue.text: Half of the gate-crashers served with a full breakfast?

indicators.note: a large part of the word is taken, its letters lying intact within it

explanation.surface: Some uninvited guests turn up for a cooked breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: The last seven letters of 'gate-crashers' give the answer; the setter calls that half.
explanation.definitionFit: Slices of bacon come with a full cooked English breakfast.

clue.text: No idea where you are? Behold the way!

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: Someone without a clue where they are is shown the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no idea of one's whereabouts is being astray.

clue.text: Is coming in about a pay increment

indicators.note: the word is enters the two-letter word for about

parts.note: re means about, concerning
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is due soon regarding a raise in salary.
explanation.definitionFit: An increase in wages is a raise, or in British usage this word.

clue.text: What one does as the years go by

definitions.text: What one does as the years go by

parts.words: What one does as the years go by
parts.note: a person grows older with time

explanation.surface: A reflection on what everyone does over time.
explanation.definitionFit: To grow old is what happens with passing years.

clue.text: Rejecting the idea of Pluto not turning up?

parts.note: Dis is the Roman name of Pluto, god of the underworld
absent, not appearing

explanation.surface: Astronomers reject the notion that Pluto has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: Pluto looks like the planet, but it is the god, Dis.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning down or sending away is rejecting.

clue.text: Shining skates, maybe

definitions.meaning: beams of light, as from a shining source
flat cartilaginous fish of which the skate is one

explanation.definitionFit: Beams of light shine, and skates belong to a family of flat fish.

clue.text: They may have to take orders, but don't have to obey them

definitions.text: They may have to take orders, but don't have to obey them

parts.words: They may have to take orders, but don't have to obey them
parts.note: couriers carry orders to someone else rather than receiving commands

explanation.surface: Some people accept instructions but are under no obligation to follow them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take orders' seems to mean obey, but it means carry them to their destination.
explanation.definitionFit: Couriers convey orders and messages without having to obey them.
